issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one. 'Being looked at sexually' implies a sexual-threat/self-directed trauma context that is not supported anywhere else in the profile and is hard to reconcile with bereavement/trauma-to-loved-one as the index trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: Within the Triggers node, the items do not form a coherent theme. 'Talking about the future' could fit grief-related loss, but 'incomprehensible chatter' and especially 'being looked at sexually' point toward very different trauma contexts, making the trigger profile internally inconsistent for a single index trauma.

vignette: Marcus Vance was sixty-three when the block party that was supposed to honor his younger brother, David, fractured his life. He had been three feet away when a sudden argument escalated into violence. The air filled with panicked shouts and overlapping voices that blurred into a single, indistinguishable roar. When Marcus knelt beside him, David was gone. Marcus knew exactly what had happened, yet the sequence refused to hold together. He tried to recount it to the first responders, but he lost the thread before he could finish. The moment carried a sharp, copper taste that clung to the back of his throat. In the months that followed, Marcus stopped mentioning David at family gatherings. He found himself stepping out of rooms when relatives began weeping over old photographs or describing their own recent grief. He also began avoiding any conversation that drifted toward what might happen next, telling his wife, Clara, he needed quiet instead of planning their autumn trip. The habit settled into his work; the newsroom, once his usual refuge, became a place of quiet exits. He turned down assignments about community violence and left early when reporters' voices merged into an unintelligible hum. The triggers did not simply echo in his mind; they actively pulled the memory forward. When a junior producer leaned across his desk to explain a future deadline, his words tumbling over one another into a dense murmur, Marcus felt his breath shorten. He knew what he had witnessed, but the language refused to surface, and the familiar metallic taste flooded his mouth, dragging the unspoken scene into his present. Every time the chatter thickened or anyone brought up what might come, the past bled back through him with equal force. He had come to believe that speaking openly would unravel him completely, so he kept his distance. His editor called him in to discuss a retrospective piece on the anniversary of the shooting. As the editor began outlining next week's editorial calendar, layering his voice with another producer's excited chatter about a future investigative series, Marcus felt his pulse spike. When he tried to explain why he could not take the assignment, he lost the thread mid-sentence, his mind slipping into the copper taste of that day. The intrusion did not allow for negotiation. Any account of profound loss or any discussion of tomorrow inevitably dragged the unspoken scene into his present, unspooling his composure until he had to leave the building. Marcus spent the following weeks pacing the perimeter of the newsroom, waiting for the overlapping voices to fade. He found himself skipping morning desk meetings, telling his staff he was chasing leads, though he spent the hours at home watching the news with the sound muted. The pattern had hardened into a cage. His marriage grew quiet, the space between him and Clara widening with every unsaid conversation about their children's graduations or the long-term care David had left behind. He had hoped to outrun the intrusion by controlling his environment, but the more he avoided the triggers, the faster they seized him. When the anniversary week arrived, Marcus stood outside the paper's archives, his hand hovering over his phone. He had finally scheduled an appointment with a trauma specialist, not because he wanted to relive the night, but because he was exhausted by the way the ordinary sounds of the future kept stealing the past. He hoped to reclaim the words he had lost, to sit with his wife without flinching, and to stop the relentless pull that turned a simple conversation into an ambush.
